cardio-chest-pressure: I recommend urgent hospital evaluation because the pressure is happening with less activity than before. A heart problem is one possibility, and being comfortable now does not settle it. We should call emergency transport; please do not drive or exert yourself.

I recommend an electrical tracing of your heart and blood tests through the emergency team. They may also look at the heart valves. We will review medicines safely with the supervising clinician; treatment for indigestion can wait until urgent causes are addressed.
cardio-febrile-cough: I recommend evaluating a lung infection, while checking how well you are breathing. The pattern can fit pneumonia, but an examination alone cannot prove the cause. We may need chest imaging and other tests before choosing treatment.

I recommend prompt help for worsening breathing, confusion, faintness or inability to keep fluids down. We will agree on treatment and a specific review plan with the supervising clinician, and explain when to seek urgent care.
cardio-orthopnea-edema: I recommend prompt evaluation of the breathing difficulty and swelling. Extra fluid affecting the lungs is a concern, but the heart, kidneys and other causes need assessment. We should discuss heart and blood tests and the safest next setting for care.

I recommend seeking urgent help if breathing worsens at rest, you faint or develop chest pressure. Please bring your medicines; we will explain any changes rather than asking you to adjust them on your own.
cardio-palpitations: I recommend recording the heart rhythm with an electrical tracing. The fluttering may be an abnormal rhythm, but its exact type is not established by how it feels. We should review medicines, stimulants and appropriate blood tests.
I recommend urgent help for fainting, chest pain or worsening breathlessness. The supervising clinician will help decide treatment and whether monitoring or specialist care is needed.
cardio-pleuritic-dyspnea: I recommend emergency assessment now because the breathlessness came on suddenly with pain on breathing. A clot in the lung is one concern; infection or a collapsed lung can sometimes cause similar symptoms. We need appropriate tests to distinguish them.
I recommend emergency transport and avoiding driving yourself. We will tell the team about your symptoms and the information you have given us; the team will explain treatment after assessing you.
cardio-presyncope: I recommend checking the blood pressure pattern and reviewing your medicines because the near-faint feeling occurs with standing. We also need to consider heart rhythm problems and other causes. Nearly fainting is different from definitely losing consciousness.

I recommend rising cautiously with support while this is being evaluated. Seek urgent help for actual fainting, chest pain, persistent symptoms or new neurologic problems. We will agree on a follow-up and medication plan with the clinician.
gi-diarrhea-dehydration: I recommend replacing fluids safely and assessing the effect of the diarrhea on your circulation. An infection is possible, but medicines and other bowel conditions may matter. We should review whether testing or supervised fluid treatment is needed.

I recommend urgent help for fainting, confusion, bloody stools, severe pain or inability to drink. We will discuss hydration, hygiene and the expected review plan; antibiotics are not automatically appropriate for every diarrheal illness.
gi-epigastric-back-pain: I recommend urgent assessment of this severe upper abdominal pain. Inflammation around the pancreas is a concern, but heart and other abdominal problems can overlap. Blood tests and selected imaging can help clarify the cause.

I recommend clinician-directed pain and fluid treatment while urgent causes are evaluated. Please do not try to manage worsening pain or repeated vomiting alone; the next step is urgent care with a clear handoff.
gi-epigastric-melena: I recommend emergency evaluation today because the black tarry stool, symptoms and supplied blood count raise concern for bleeding. Ibuprofen can injure the stomach lining. We should stop it and discuss safer pain treatment with the clinician.

I recommend blood tests and specialist assessment, with an examination of the stomach using a camera when it is safe. That can help identify the source and guide treatment. Your family concern deserves attention, but we cannot diagnose cancer from these symptoms. Vomiting blood or fainting needs immediate help.
gi-progressive-dysphagia: I recommend investigating the swallowing difficulty and weight change. Inflammation, narrowing and other conditions can make food stick; we should not assume the cause from age alone. A specialist may need to examine the esophagus with a camera and take appropriate samples.

I recommend urgent help if food becomes stuck and you cannot swallow saliva, or if you develop breathing trouble. We will explain the referral and how to contact us while waiting; please tell us if intake is getting harder.
gi-right-lower-pain: I recommend urgent evaluation of the pain that has moved to the right lower abdomen. Appendicitis is one possibility; pregnancy-related and urinary problems can overlap. A pregnancy test and selected blood or imaging tests can guide the next steps.

I recommend that we involve the supervising clinician now. Please report worsening pain, faintness or vomiting immediately. A belief that pregnancy is unlikely is not the same as a negative test; we will explain why testing matters.
gi-right-upper-pain: I recommend urgent assessment because this pain has lasted for hours with fever. An inflamed gallbladder is a concern. We need an ultrasound and blood tests to clarify what is happening; I cannot yet tell you whether surgery will be needed.

I recommend that the emergency and surgical team guide treatment if that concern is confirmed. We will review pain relief and fluids safely, and consider other causes when appropriate. Worsening pain, faintness or yellowing of the eyes needs prompt attention.
neuro-acute-focal-weakness: I recommend an emergency stroke assessment now. Sudden arm weakness and speech difficulty need immediate attention even if some symptoms improve. The team needs the last time you were normal and will arrange urgent imaging and glucose assessment.

I recommend emergency transport; please do not drive. We cannot confirm a stroke subtype here or decide treatment from appearance alone. I will communicate the timing and findings to the team without delaying care.
neuro-back-bladder-redflags: I recommend emergency assessment because the new bladder difficulty with back and leg symptoms can signal pressure on important nerves. We need urgent specialist assessment and appropriate imaging; this should not wait for a routine back-pain visit.

I recommend prompt help if weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel function worsens. We will explain each examination and respect refusals. We should defer routine manipulation while urgent causes are being assessed.
neuro-distal-neuropathy: I recommend evaluating the pattern of numbness and burning in both feet. Diabetes, vitamin problems and medicines are among the possibilities; the distribution and specific examination findings help guide testing.

I recommend protecting your feet, checking for injury and discussing safe symptom treatment with the clinician. Please seek prompt help for new weakness, rapid change or an injury you cannot feel; we will arrange review of the testing and foot-care plan.
neuro-positional-vertigo: I recommend assessing whether the brief, position-triggered spinning comes from the balance system in the inner ear. A positional maneuver can help when it is safe for your neck. We must consider other causes if the pattern or neurologic findings are concerning.

I recommend assistance when you feel unsteady and avoiding driving while dizzy. Seek urgent help for new weakness, speech difficulty, a severe new headache or continuous worsening symptoms. We will discuss an appropriate maneuver and follow-up with the clinician.
neuro-recurrent-headache: I recommend comparing this headache carefully with your usual episodes. Migraine is a possibility, but a changed pattern or new warning sign requires another approach. We should review how often you use headache medicines before choosing treatment.

I recommend prompt help for sudden maximal pain, fever with neck stiffness, fainting or new neurologic symptoms. We can discuss a headache record, safe medicine use and follow-up; please tell us if the usual pattern changes.
neuro-thunderclap-headache: I recommend emergency assessment now because the headache reached maximum intensity so quickly and differs from your usual migraine. Bleeding around the brain is a concern, but we need urgent imaging and specialist assessment to know more.

I recommend emergency transport and no driving. Depending on the timing and imaging result, the team may discuss additional tests. Please report any change in alertness or neurologic symptoms immediately; we should not do neck manipulation while this is being evaluated.
renal-acute-retention: I recommend urgent assessment of the inability to empty your bladder. Medicines, blockage and nerve problems can contribute. The clinician may need to measure retained urine and relieve the pressure while looking for a cause.

I recommend bringing the names and doses of new medicines. Please report fever, worsening pain or new leg or saddle-area symptoms immediately. A proposed bladder scan or catheter does not mean a result has already been obtained.
renal-colicky-flank: I recommend checking for a stone or another cause of blockage, while looking carefully for infection. Wave-like pain can fit a stone, but fever with an obstructed kidney needs urgent treatment. Appropriate urine tests and imaging can help.

I recommend clinician-directed relief for pain and nausea. Seek urgent help for fever, inability to urinate, persistent vomiting or worsening symptoms. Hydration alone is not enough if an infected blockage is suspected.
renal-dysuria: I recommend evaluating a bladder infection while considering other causes of burning. Urine testing and pregnancy information may affect the safest treatment. We should not infer a test result just from the symptoms.
I recommend prompt help if fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening illness develops. We will discuss treatment, your allergies and when to check back if symptoms do not improve.
renal-flank-pain: I recommend evaluating a kidney infection because the urinary symptoms are accompanied by fever and flank pain. We should check urine and pregnancy testing and decide whether you can safely drink and take treatment outside the hospital.

I recommend that the clinician choose an antibiotic that reaches kidney tissue, taking your sulfa reaction and pregnancy possibility into account. Fever with a blockage, instability or inability to keep fluids down needs emergency evaluation. Otherwise we should review you and culture results within 48 to 72 hours.
renal-luts-nocturia: I recommend clarifying whether you are passing large volumes or needing to empty often, and how discomfort relates to the bladder filling. Bladder irritation, caffeine and metabolic causes can overlap. Appropriate urine and blood tests may help.

I recommend reviewing fluid and caffeine intake and arranging follow-up for the results and symptom pattern. Please seek prompt care for fever, visible blood, inability to urinate or marked worsening.
renal-painless-hematuria: I recommend investigating the visible blood even though it is painless. We need to clarify whether the blood comes from the urine and consider kidney, bladder and other causes. Urine microscopy and selected tests can help guide referral.

I recommend prompt help for heavy bleeding, clots with inability to urinate, faintness or worsening illness. We will explain the test and referral plan and make sure you know how to obtain the results.
